new_statements.quote: In dissyllabic words the accent is generally on the first syllable even when the last syllable is checked, e. gr., [example garbled in scanned: 'Ujd'], a cloth; reled', squeeze. There are few exceptions to this rule. They must be learned by practice. I have so far not ascertained the reason of the accentuation of the last syllable in those words. In general it may be said that accentuation is by far not as pronounced as in German or English. Barring some very short vowels, the accentuated has hardly more stress than the non-accentuated syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Hoffmann (1903:4): accent generally on the first syllable of disyllables, even when the final syllable ends in a checked consonant; a few lexical exceptions have final accent; the accent is phonetically weak. This is one side of a documented conflict for the same language: Nottrott 1882:6 also puts the accent on the first syllable (infinitives and diphthong-final words antepenult); Langendoen 1963:14-16 derives a right-edge alternating pattern with penult de-accenting before a single consonant; Gumperz & Biligiri 1957:8-9 (via the Stanford Phonology Archive sheet) call stress predictable, evenly distributed, last syllable slightly stronger; Sinha 1975 and Osada 2008 (reported by Horo et al. 2023) put prominence on the second syllable; Horo, Gogoi & Anderson 2023 (instrumental) find no reliable word-level cue, duration marking utterance right edges and intensity tending to peak on the second syllable. No single fixed-position reading is supported by the open sources taken together.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Hoffmann says nothing about secondary stress. Langendoen 1963 Rule 19 assigns an alternating '(2)1..21' pattern (secondary stress on alternate vowels leftward from the main stress). Horo et al. 2023 report secondary intensity peaks on the final syllable of tetra- and pentasyllables in sentential frames.
new_statements.exceptions: Hoffmann: 'few exceptions' with accent on the last syllable, reason not ascertained, to be learned by practice. Nottrott: infinitive forms and words ending in a diphthong take the accent on the antepenult (kajitea, kajikedae).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolated words (Hoffmann's disyllables). Horo et al. 2023 show that the one robust cue, duration, belongs to the utterance/phrase right edge, not the word; their word-level results come from words in isolation and in carrier/focus frames.
new_statements.identity_note: mund1321 'Munda' [unx] is a Glottolog bookkeeping code, not a distinct language: Glottolog 5.3 states that Munda [unx] and Mundari [unr] 'are part of the same language (Cook 1965, Grierson 1906, Osada & Onishi 2012)', and the ISO change request 2007-065 that created [unx] split it from Mundari on census enumeration and ethnonym grounds alone, citing no linguistic description. The only descriptive literature is therefore that of Mundari, glottocode mund1320 (Hasada/Naguri/Kera/Tamaria varieties, Jharkhand), which is already in the catalog as a 'conflict' record (Hoffmann 1903 initial vs Cook 1965 / Sinha 1975 / Osada 2008 / Horo et al. 2023). Adding mund1321 would double-count one entity; the correct action is to mark mund1321 as an alias of mund1320 rather than to create a record.

new_statements.quote: [p. 100] Multi-syllabic morphemes are combinations of CV and CVC syllables. These patterns are accompanied by stress in accordance with the following rule" Stress:"If the final syllable of a morpheme is closed(CVC), then the final syllable is accented; If the final syllable is open (CV),then the preceding,or penultimate syllable is accented." This rule applies to stress within morphemes. Stress patterns in words would take further investigation. In general, stress tends to remain with the primary roots, with the formative elements generally unstressed. [p. 286] Open syllables are CV, closed syllables are CVC, but zero onset is allowed. Final closed syllables are stressed, but elsewhere stress is on the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record for mund1321 (in_catalog false); the only existing statement is Hoffmann 1903 p. 4: in disyllables the accent is 'generally on the first syllable even when the last syllable is checked', with a few unexplained exceptions. Cook agrees with Hoffmann for CV-final disyllables (first = penultimate syllable) but differs exactly on closed-final forms: Hoffmann keeps initial stress 'even when the last syllable is checked', whereas Cook stresses a closed (CVC) final syllable. Cook's is a weight-sensitive final/penult rule, Hoffmann's an initial-default rule for disyllables. Cook does not discuss Hoffmann's accent remark in his section on 'The Work of Hoffmann' (no accent/st…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Within the morpheme, stress falls on the final syllable if it is closed (CVC) and on the penultimate syllable if the final syllable is open (CV); i.e. a right-edge, coda-weight-sensitive rule (final if heavy, else penult). In polymorphemic words stress tends to stay on the primary root, with affixes/formatives unstressed; Cook says word-level stress patterns need further investigation. He also notes (p. 92) that the diphthongs /ai/, /au/, which occur in open syllables in final or non-final position, 'are generally stressed'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress. Sentence-level 'emphatic stress' and intonation contours are treated separately in the syntax (question/vocative patterns, pp. 253-256), not as word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Domain caveat: the rule is stated for morphemes; for words Cook only offers the tendency that stress remains on primary roots and formatives are unstressed, and flags word stress as needing further study. Diphthongs /ai/ /au/ (open syllables) are 'generally stressed' even when non-final (p. 92), which he does not reconcile with the closed-final rule. No lexical exceptions listed.
new_statements.identity_note: mund1321 'Munda' [unx] is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid: ISO 639-3 CR 2007-065 split muw into unr Mundari and unx Munda on census/ethnonym grounds, and Glottolog treats them as one language (citing Cook 1965 among others). Cook 1965 describes Mundari (mund1320) as spoken in Chota Nagpur, south Bihar; his fieldwork was in Singhbhum District 1953-1962 with informant Menas Orea of Buruma (one of Hoffmann's Encyclopaedia Mundarica informants). He recognises two dialects, Hasada (no phonemic aspiration) and Naguri (phonemic aspiration, Hindi/Sadri loans), and regards Ho as effectively a Mundari dialect; he does not label his stress rule as dialect-specific.

readall_conflicts: Cook 1965 (pp. 100, 286) and Hoffmann 1903 (p. 4, the existing statement) disagree on disyllables with a closed final syllable: Hoffmann says the accent is generally on the first syllable 'even when the last syllable is checked' (with a few exceptions he could not explain), while Cook states that a closed (CVC) final syllable of a morpheme is stressed and only open-final morphemes take penultimate stress. For open-final disyllables the two coincide (initial = penultimate). Cook restricts his rule to the morpheme and says word-level stress needs further investigation (stress tends to stay on primary roots, formatives unstressed), so part of the gap may be domain (Hoffmann speaks of 'words'). No other work was listed for this item; the earlier mund1321 notes that the record of substance lives under mund1320 Mundari with classification conflict, and Cook's statement adds a third, weight-sensitive position to that disagreement rather than resolving it.

sources.citation: Crothers, Lorentz, Sherman & Vihman (eds.). 1979. Handbook of Phonological Data from a Sample of the World's Languages (Stanford Phonology Archive), pp. 237-239 'Mundari', quoting Gumperz & Biligiri 1957, Notes on the phonology of Mundari, Indian Linguistics 17: 6-15.
sources.note: STRESS field quotes Gumperz & Biligiri 1957:8-9: 'In single word utterances length and stress are predictable and therefore not phonemic. In words of more than one syllable stress is fairly evenly distributed. The last syllable is slightly more stressed than the rest, although occasionally in the same word, stress may be on the first syllable in one occurrence and on the second in another.' Second-hand (archive sheet) for the 1957 article.

sources.citation: Langendoen, D. Terence. 1963 [rekeyed 2010]. Mundari phonology. Unpublished ms., Munda Languages Project (Univ. of Chicago, 1962 fieldwork), 17 pp; author copy on his Arizona page.
sources.note: pp. 14-16 (scanned file lines 600-656): Rules 17-21 derive stress: every vowel is [+acc] (17); a penultimate vowel followed by exactly one consonant loses its accent (18), so /baranda/ and /gel+Ea/ [géléa] keep penult accent but CVCV(C) words do not; Rule 19 'assigns an alternating (2)1..21 stress pattern to vowels within words' with main stress on the last accented vowel; Rule 20 'reduces stress on a final /a/, provided it is not preceded by an unaccented vowel'. A right-edge, weight-conditioned alternating analysis, opposite to Hoffmann's initial accent.

sources.note: Nothing linguistic at all. Rationale is census/ethnonym only ('Munda is regarded as a separate language from Mundari by numerous published sources. Munda and Mundari are enumerated separately on the national census'); sources listed are Krishna 1991, India Missions Association 1997 (x2), K.S. Singh 1993, 1994 — no grammar or phonology. Confirms that no descriptive source for a distinct 'Munda [unx]' exists.
